No third-party tools. No custom work. I scored 65 products on 19 semantic capabilities, and the results surprised me.

Semantic Context Index: 65 products, 19 capabilities, one heatmap [...] Ask your shiny new data agent a simple question: “What was revenue last quarter?”

It answers in two seconds. The SQL looks clean. The number is wrong.

Revenue at your company excludes refunds. It counts the order date, not the ship date. It lives as a measure in a Power BI model, a metric in dbt, and a sentence in a Confluence page nobody updated since 2024. The agent saw none of that. It saw a column called `amount` and did its best. [...] I’ve built a few text-to-SQL agents on Snowflake and Denodo. Every project hit the same wall around week three. The model works. The plumbing works. The answers drift, because the agent has no idea what the business means by its own words.

The fix has a name. People call it a semantic layer, an ontology, a knowledge graph, or…

results.content:
Data handling is a second reason to choose it. Geodd does not use API data for model training, and it does not store prompts, outputs, or uploaded files unless separately agreed in writing. The models listed below also state zero data retention by default. The company is GDPR ready, and its SOC 2 compliance is pending.

If your agent is written in code, the model API is the platform decision that sets both your bill and your reliability.

### Pricing [...] ### Who it suits

Make suits solo operators, small agencies, and startups that want lots of connectors at a low monthly price. It is also a reasonable step up from a basic automation tool when you want to add a model without learning a new paradigm.

It is less suited to deep multi-agent systems. If your agents must coordinate and be tracked as a group, a dedicated agent platform fits better.

Make is where you go when integrations and price matter more than agent sophistication.

### Pricing [...] Comparison of an agent's orchestration layer and inference layer, each with four points and a verdict.

Every agent has two layers. The orchestration layer is where you define instructions, connect apps, set triggers, and watch runs. The inference layer is the model API that does the reasoning on each step. Some products bundle both, while others give you only one.

Pick the builder for how your team works, and pick the model layer for what each run costs and where your data goes.

results.title: Stack AI Alternatives: 8 Governed Agent Platforms
results.content:
An agent remembering context is different from an app storing workflow state. Context lives in a conversation or a prompt, costs tokens to refill, and disappears when the session ends. App state lives in tables with a schema, survives restarts, and can be read by people and other systems. If a platform only offers the first, the work is not stateful. This is the core of governance at the point agents act. [...] This is the app layer in an agent architecture: the agent reasoned once about how to handle intake, and the app runs the repeatable checks on every row afterward. Build this on Major.

## The Major take

The constraint is simple. An agent that re-reasons stable steps on every run makes repeated work depend on model behavior and on whatever context survived the last conversation. Cost tracks usage, and the audit trail is whatever the prompt happened to log. [...] Jason Bao··Updated

The best Stack AI alternatives are Major, n8n, UiPath, Microsoft Copilot Studio, Voiceflow, Relevance AI, Gumloop, and Dify, and Major is the one to evaluate first if your agents will touch real systems. Stack AI is a visual builder for agent workflows. Major is the enterprise platform where agents build the software they run on: an agent works out a repeatable step once, builds a deterministic app for it, and runs that app from then on.
